What it costs if you leave it on

With Amazon\'s launcher on, Home goes through Amazon\'s home screen again: its ads and a flash of it on every press. This also turns on \"Warn if the system undoes Debloat\", which is what shows the tile in step 3.

What the TV shows after a few idle minutes. Off: nothing, and the TV sleeps on its own timer. Colours: Android\'s changing colours. Amazon\'s: the TV\'s own one, which carries ads. Salotto\'s idle clock is separate and only runs on its own home screen. Press OK for the next choice.
The language Live TV picks when a channel has several soundtracks, from the next channel change on. Press OK for the next language.

The Stick goes to sleep by itself after 15 minutes without a button press. Off, it sleeps only when the TV does (the switches above) or when you put it to sleep.
Takes the picture in from the edges, for a TV that crops them. Leave it off when the TV shows the picture 1:1 (for example in Film mode), or black borders appear.
How far in from each edge, the same on all four sides. Press OK for the next step; it wraps round to 0. Turning Overscan off sets it back to 0.

Only the steps this TV will not let the app do itself

Switch on Settings, My Fire TV, Developer options, ADB debugging. Then from a computer with Android platform-tools installed:

adb connect %1$s

The TV will ask you to allow the connection.

Fire OS has no menu for this, so it is switched on over ADB. "Finish setup automatically" in Setup does it from the TV, or run:

adb shell settings put secure enabled_accessibility_services %1$s/%1$s.HomeRedirectService
adb shell settings put secure accessibility_enabled 1
One command makes every row on the TV Health page changeable from the remote, permanently:\n\nadb shell pm grant %1$s android.permission.WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS

Without this, Amazon\'s home screen shows for a moment on each Home press, and Home does nothing while Amazon\'s home screen is already showing. Salotto uses it only to spot the Home press in the system log:\n\nadb shell pm grant %1$s android.permission.READ_LOGS

Every one of these is undone with:
adb shell pm enable <package>

Nothing is uninstalled and no data is deleted. The Debloat page lists what each package does. Alexa and everything else marked caution are left out here because they change how the TV behaves - choose those individually.

%1$d of the listed packages can still be switched off. Debloat can switch them off one at a time or all at once, and put them back the same way. Packages Fire OS refuses are counted as protected once Debloat has tried them.
\n\nA few telemetry packages are protected by Fire OS and cannot be switched off by any app, even with the privacy switches above off.
Switching these off removes Alexa: no voice search, no voice timers, and the microphone button on the remote stops doing anything. Everything else keeps working.
ADB link - open Setup to connect

Each item is switched off with \"pm disable-user\", which leaves the app and its data on the TV and is undone with \"pm enable\". Disabling does not free storage; what you get back is memory and processor time.

Marked risky: it is never switched off by the one-press buttons and it is offered only on a TV that would then send Home straight to Salotto (not Fire OS 7, where Amazon\'s Home Starter takes Home). Switching it off takes two presses. To switch it back on, use this row, \"Undo everything this app switched off\", or from a computer: adb shell pm enable --user 0 %1$s\n\nSwitch it back on before you uninstall Salotto, or the TV is left with no home screen until a computer switches it on.
Marked caution: switching it off changes how the TV behaves.

Anything the system is currently using as a keyboard, a TV input, a home screen, a device administrator or an accessibility service is locked, and so is a short list of components the TV cannot start without. Everything else is yours to switch off - reversibly.

Turning it off sends Home back to Amazon\'s home screen straight away, and \"Re-apply after reboot\" stops while it is off. To turn it back on, run \"Finish setup automatically\" in Setup (ADB debugging must still be on), or use \"Commands for a computer\". Press twice to confirm.
What this launcher needs, and how to switch it on

Fire OS does not list Salotto under Settings, Accessibility, so the redirect is switched on over the TV's debugging connection: from this TV with "Finish setup automatically" below, or from a computer with "Commands for a computer".

Without it, Salotto still works as an app you open yourself; only the Home button needs it.

If the Home button ever goes back to Amazon's home screen, for example after an update, run "Finish setup automatically" again.
Let this app configure the TV

This switches on the Home button redirect. It also lets the app switch off Amazon's advertising and telemetry packages and turn off the animations, if you choose to.

Fire OS runs its debugging service on the television itself, so with your permission this app can connect to it and gain the same access a computer would have. The connection never leaves the TV. The TELEVISION, not this app, asks you to approve a key - check that the fingerprint it shows matches the one here, and tick "Always allow" so it is not asked again.

A direct connection will be refused, and not because anything is wrong: recent Fire OS builds drop any ADB connection that starts on the TV itself. "On-device tunnel" gets around that block from inside the app - no computer needed. If you would rather not, "Commands for a computer" lists exactly what to run instead.
Open \"My Fire TV\" (ADB debugging lives here)
Deleting our key here stops this app using the link. The TV keeps its own copy until you use \"Revoke ADB authorisations\" under My Fire TV, Developer options.

Fire OS refuses ADB connections that start on the TV, so the app reaches its own debugging service the way a computer would - through a local VPN that presents an outside-looking address. It routes only its own private subnet, stays entirely on this TV, and makes no internet connection. Turning it on shows the system\'s VPN prompt once and a key icon in the status bar; the first connect asks you to approve the key on the TV.\n\nIt only comes up while the app is actively configuring the TV and shuts off again within seconds of finishing (\"ready\" means enabled but down, \"active\" means up right now). While it is up, the TV\'s own ADB is reachable to apps on this device again - they would still each need you to approve their key on screen, so approve ONLY prompts you expected. Needs \"ADB debugging\" left on under My Fire TV; turn that off when you are done for the tightest setup. Reversible any time, and Amazon may re-block it in a future update.

Fire OS doesn\'t list Salotto in its Accessibility menu, so the app switches it on itself, through the TV\'s own debugging service. No computer needed.

Press Set it up and approve two prompts: a VPN notice, then the TV\'s key prompt. Tick \"Always allow\" on the second

Android\'s VPN notice says the app could monitor network traffic; Salotto\'s only carries the TV\'s own debugging connection, and nothing leaves the TV. In each prompt, press Down to reach OK. No Developer options? Open My Fire TV, then About, and press Select on the device name seven times. To do this later, press Continue; you can still open Salotto from Amazon\'s app row.
Let the app clean up your TV

To switch Amazon\'s packages off, the app needs the access a computer has over ADB - so it makes a private connection to the TV\'s own service. No computer, no account, and nothing ever leaves the TV.
